submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires on the token that completes a stative, generic or passive predicate about an abstract, non-physical subject (a task, question, decision, action, problem, work, rule, price or quantity), typically built from a high-frequency general-purpose verb - do, make, take, answer, solve, apply, occur, happen, rise, be true, be forthcoming - as in 'no action was taken', 'little progress was made', 'the work is done', 'the question was answered', 'the problem was solved', 'no explanation was forthcoming', 'this is true of the iron cross', 'the same rules apply to everyone'. It stays near zero when the same predicate word takes a physical object or a specific event as subject ('the phone was answered', 'the dishes were done', 'the house was sold'), when the clause is active or agentive ('they took no action', 'he answered all the questions'), or when a lexically specific verb replaces the general one ('the work was sold', 'the decision was announced', 'the matter was resolved').

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Every five years, the regional water authority reviews the condition of its treatment plants, pump stations, and distribution mains. The process begins in January, when engineers compile maintenance logs from the previous cycle and flag any components that failed more often than expected. Those flags are sorted by risk, and the highest-risk assets receive a detailed physical inspection. Inspectors typically work in pairs, carrying ultrasonic gauges and chloride test kits, and they record their findings in a shared database that the planning office can query at any time.

The review is not only a technical exercise. It also involves ratepayers, local councils, and the state environmental regulator, all of whom have an interest in how the authority spends its capital budget. The authority holds public meetings in each of the four service districts, and residents can submit written comments for thirty days after the last meeting. In the previous cycle, roughly two hundred comments arrived, most of them about discoloration in the eastern district and a persistent pressure problem on the ridge road. Staff replied to each comment individually and published a summary of the responses on the authority's website. The regulator also conducts its own audit every third year, checking chlorine residual records, backflow prevention certificates, and the calibration logs for every analyzer in the system. Staff share the audit findings with the board before they draft the capital plan.

Drought years complicate the picture. When reservoir levels fall below sixty percent of capacity, the authority must weigh new supply projects against conservation measures, and the board often asks for a revised ranking before it votes. Last summer the eastern reservoir dropped to forty-one percent, the lowest reading since the monitoring program began in 1987. Staff proposed a temporary connection to the neighboring county's system, which the board approved after a short debate. The connection has since been used twice and performed as expected.

Once the technical and public phases are complete, the planning office prepares a draft capital plan. The draft lists every proposed project, its estimated cost, and the year in which construction would begin. Projects are ranked using a scoring system that weighs public safety, environmental compliance, and cost effectiveness. The board then reviews the ranking, sometimes moving a project up or down by a year or two, and votes on the final plan in September.

The most recent cycle produced a plan of moderate size. It funded the replacement of two aging clarifiers, a new booster pump for the northern district, and several miles of pipe along the ridge road. It also set aside money for a pilot study of membrane filtration, which staff believe could reduce treatment costs over the long run. The board debated the pilot study at length, since its benefits are uncertain and the authority would bear its costs immediately. In the end, the study survived by a single vote.

Implementation now falls to the engineering department, which will issue design contracts over the winter and begin construction in the spring. The department has promised quarterly progress reports to the board, and the regulator has asked for an annual compliance summary. No further changes were made to the inspection schedule, so the next full review will begin on the same timetable as this one, with the first site visits scheduled for the second week of January.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The feature sits deep inside a long technical passage: passive 'were made' about the abstract subject 'changes', testing whether the pole still fires when the completing clause is far from the input's start.
